lesson_title: The Photograph by Age Rows: Reading a Population Pyramid
hook_text: Photograph a whole country in rows by age, and the shape of the crowd predicts its future.
clip_script: Imagine photographing the whole country at once — sixty-odd million people — arranged by a strict photographer. Everyone lines up in rows by AGE: babies and toddlers in the front row, five-to-nines behind them, row upon row, until the eldest citizens stand at the very back. Males left of the centre aisle, females right. Now climb a ladder and look straight down. The OUTLINE of that crowd is the population pyramid. A packed front row shrinking to sparse back rows: a land of children, growing fast. Rows of nearly equal length: a steady country. A front row SHORTER than the rows behind it: a nation that has slowed its baby-making — that is Japan and South Korea, and it means shrinking. And the photograph is an archive. A row oddly shorter than its neighbours — like a bite out of the crowd — marks a generation thinned by war, epidemic or famine. A bulging row marks a baby boom. The back rows lean female, because women outlive men nearly everywhere. South Africa's crowd? Broad in front, but no longer widening — and with one huge feature: a massive block of people in their twenties and thirties. Demographers call it a dividend. It pays out on one condition: that bulge must find work.
visual_style: An impossible aerial shot of a nation-sized crowd arranged in age rows; the camera rises until the crowd resolves into a pyramid silhouette; bites and bulges highlight in sequence; ends on South Africa's outline with its glowing young-adult bulge.
mood: Awe-inspiring scale with a sharp final message.
pacing: Slow rise to the reveal, quick tour of shapes and scars, pointed one-condition ending.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson for the five indicators and the three pyramid shapes.
